facts.body: The name derives from the Old East Slavic or Old Russian word ukraina , meaning "borderland," which was used to describe the area on medieval Russia's border at the time of the Tatar invasion in the 13th century

facts.title: Why it is called Uganda
facts.body: The name is derived from the Swahili word u , meaning "land" or "country," and the Ganda people; the origin of the Ganda name is unclear

facts.title: Why it is called United States
facts.body: The name America was first used in 1507 and is derived from the first name of Amerigo VESPUCCI (1454-1512), an Italian explorer, navigator, and cartographer; the name United States first appeared in a document subtitle during the discussions that led to the Declaration of Independence in 1776

facts.title: Why it is called Uruguay
facts.body: Name derives from the Uruguay River, which makes up the western border of the country; the river's name comes from the Guarani words uru (bird) and guay (tail)

facts.title: Why it is called Uzbekistan
facts.body: The name comes from the local people, the Uzbeks, whose name is said to have originated with Mongol leader Ghiyath ad-Din Muhammad UZBEK; the Persian suffix - stan means "country"

facts.title: Why it is called Vatican City
facts.body: "holy" comes from the Greek word hera , meaning "sacred"; "see" comes from the Latin word sedes , meaning "seat," and refers to the episcopal chair; the name Vatican derives from the hill Mons Vaticanus on which the Vatican is located and which comes from the Latin vates (prophet), referring to the fortune tellers and soothsayers who frequented the area in Roman times

facts.title: Why it is called Saint Vincent and the Grenadines
facts.body: Explorer Christopher COLUMBUS named the island after Saint VINCENT of Saragossa because 22 January 1498, the day of discovery, was the saint's feast day

facts.title: Why it is called Venezuela
facts.body: In 1499, the stilt-houses built on Lake Maracaibo reminded explorers Alonso de OJEDA and Amerigo VESPUCCI of buildings in Venice, Italy, and they named the region "Venezuola," meaning "Little Venice"

facts.title: Why it is called Vietnam
facts.body: The name translates as "Viet south;" Viet is an ethnic term of unknown origin that dates back to ancient times, and nam (south) refers to the country's location

facts.title: Why it is called Vanuatu
facts.body: The name means "Our land forever" in several of the Austronesian languages spoken on the islands; the former name, New Hebrides, was given by Captain James COOK in 1774 because he thought they looked similar to the Hebrides islands off the coast of Scotland

facts.title: Why it is called Samoa
facts.body: The name's meaning and origin are unclear; some assert that it can mean "place of the moa bird" of Polynesian mythology, or it could be a local chieftain's name

facts.title: Why it is called Yemen
facts.body: The name origin is unclear but may come from the Arabic word al-yamin , meaning "the right," as a reference to its geographic position in relation to Mecca

facts.title: Why it is called South Africa
facts.body: Self-descriptive name from the country's location on the continent; "Africa" is derived from the Roman designation of the area corresponding to present-day Tunisia "Africa terra," which meant "Land of the Afri" (the tribe resident in that area), but which eventually came to mean the entire continent

facts.title: Why it is called Zambia
facts.body: Name is derived from the Zambezi River, which flows through the western part of the country and forms the southern border with Zimbabwe

facts.title: Why it is called Zimbabwe
facts.body: Takes its name from the Kingdom of Zimbabwe (13th-15th century) and its capital of Great Zimbabwe, which was built of stone; the name Zimbabwe comes from the Bantu phrase zimba we bahwe , meaning "houses of stones;" the former name, Rhodesia, was derived from the name of British colonial administrator Cecil RHODES

facts.title: The furthest you can get from land
facts.body: Point Nemo lies in the South Pacific, about 2,688 km from its nearest land. Its three closest neighbours are tiny islands near Pitcairn, Easter Island and Antarctica.

facts.title: A sea with no coastline
facts.body: The Sargasso Sea has boundaries made by ocean currents rather than land. Those moving currents surround a floating seaweed habitat in the North Atlantic.

facts.title: A valley that takes up a country-sized slice
facts.body: Andorra’s Madriu-Perafita-Claror Valley covers about 9% of the whole country. Its mountain landscape still reflects a communal land-ownership tradition dating to the 13th century.

facts.title: Desert irrigation with Iron Age roots
facts.body: At Al Ain’s Hili sites, evidence survives of early aflaj irrigation. These engineered water channels helped sustain settled life in a desert landscape thousands of years ago.

facts.title: A Buddhist crossroads
facts.body: Long before its modern borders, Afghanistan was a meeting place of Buddhist artistic traditions. The Bamiyan Valley preserves monasteries and sanctuaries spanning centuries of that history.

facts.title: A harbour designed by nature
facts.body: Antigua’s deep, narrow bays and surrounding hills made a natural hurricane shelter for sailing ships. That geography helped determine where the British built their naval dockyard, using enslaved African labour.

facts.title: One town, several civilizations
facts.body: At Butrint, a walk through the ruins passes through a Greek colony, a Roman city and a bishopric. Marshes eventually helped bring this once-busy town to abandonment.

facts.title: Medieval book-making schools
facts.body: Sanahin monastery was famous for its calligraphers and manuscript illuminators. These Armenian monasteries were centres of learning as well as places of worship.

facts.title: A capital built around a sacred tree
facts.body: Mbanza Kongo was a capital of the Kingdom of Kongo. Its historic centre grew around a royal residence, a court and a holy tree, placing sacred and political landmarks together.

facts.title: Trees older than the Roman Empire
facts.body: The alerce trees protected in Los Alerces National Park belong to a species that can live for more than 3,600 years. Some Patagonian forests are living records measured in millennia.

facts.title: A zoo in an imperial garden
facts.body: Schönbrunn’s palace gardens contain the zoo founded in 1752. The grounds bring an imperial residence and an extraordinarily long zoological history into the same place.

facts.title: An annual meeting of ocean giants
facts.body: Whale sharks gather at Western Australia’s Ningaloo Coast every year. The same protected landscape also has a hidden world of underground caves and streams beneath the land.

facts.title: A forest with a prehistoric pedigree
facts.body: The Hyrcanian forests shared by Azerbaijan and Iran trace their history back 25–50 million years. They are remnants of forests that once spread much more widely across northern temperate regions.

facts.title: A cave full of living fossils
facts.body: Vjetrenica Cave shelters animals whose nearest relatives disappeared long ago. It is also home to the only known subterranean tubeworm described in UNESCO’s account of the site.

facts.title: A city that refused the grid
facts.body: Bridgetown’s historic streets curve and wind. That layout sets it apart from the orderly grids used for many Spanish and Dutch colonial cities in the Caribbean.

facts.title: Tiger country at the edge of the sea
facts.body: The Sundarbans is a maze of tidal channels and salt-tolerant mangroves where Bengal tigers live alongside crocodiles. A tiger habitat does not have to look like an inland jungle.

facts.title: Lifts for boats
facts.body: Belgium’s historic Canal du Centre has four hydraulic boat lifts. They are the surviving examples of their era that UNESCO identifies as remaining in their original working condition.

facts.title: Iron-making before the Roman Empire
facts.body: At Douroula, evidence of iron production dates to the eighth century BCE. Burkina Faso’s heritage sites also preserve standing furnaces from later iron-working traditions.

facts.title: Half-human, half-plant sculptures
facts.body: Inside the ancient Thracian tomb at Sveshtari, ten carved female figures blend human and plant forms. The tomb dates to the third century BCE but was only discovered in 1982.

facts.title: Thousands of ancient towers for the dead
facts.body: Bahrain’s Dilmun heritage site includes roughly 11,774 burial mounds. Many were originally low cylindrical towers, built between about 2200 and 1750 BCE.

facts.title: Drumming with a moving centre
facts.body: Burundi’s royal-drum ritual combines percussion, dancing, songs and heroic poetry. Drums form a semicircle around a central drum, with some performers dancing to the ensemble’s rhythm.

facts.title: A last stronghold for West African lions
facts.body: Benin shares the W-Arly-Pendjari protected complex with Burkina Faso and Niger. UNESCO identifies it as the home of the region’s only viable lion population.

facts.title: A neighbourhood over the river
facts.body: Kampong Ayer is a large settlement of houses on stilts over the Brunei River. Wooden walkways link parts of the community, while boats connect it to the surrounding city.

facts.title: A mountain that powered an industry
facts.body: In the 1500s, Potosí was an enormous silver-production centre. Artificial lakes and aqueducts supplied water to mills processing ore from Cerro Rico—the “Rich Mountain.”

facts.title: Brazil has more than rainforest
facts.body: The Cerrado is an ancient tropical savannah ecosystem. Its protected areas have sheltered species through past climate shifts, making this less-famous Brazilian landscape a remarkable refuge.

facts.title: A pirate-friendly address
facts.body: The Bahamas’ position beside busy shipping lanes helped piracy flourish in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries. Its island geography made it useful for more than beach holidays.

facts.title: A dance inspired by a vision
facts.body: Drametse’s famous masked drum dance traces its origin to a sixteenth-century religious vision. The tradition spread to other parts of Bhutan and became a major expression of its cultural heritage.

facts.title: An art gallery in the desert
facts.body: Tsodilo holds more than 4,500 rock paintings in just 10 square kilometres of the Kalahari. The landscape records human activity stretching back at least 100,000 years.

facts.title: A castle made from ten buildings
facts.body: Nesvizh Castle is an interconnected complex of ten buildings arranged around a six-sided courtyard. Its owners helped turn the town into a centre of art, science and craftsmanship.

facts.title: A reef on a continental scale
facts.body: Belize’s coast forms part of the largest barrier reef in the Northern Hemisphere. The protected system includes not just coral, but atolls, mangroves, lagoons and hundreds of sandy cays.

facts.title: Tropical-sea fossils in Quebec
facts.body: Anticosti Island preserves marine fossils spanning roughly ten million years around Earth’s first major animal mass extinction. Today’s Canadian island was once beneath an ancient tropical sea.

facts.title: A rainforest reached by water
facts.body: Salonga, described by UNESCO as Africa’s largest tropical rainforest reserve, is so isolated that access is by water. It protects animals such as bonobos and Congo peacocks.

facts.title: A landscape that switches habitats
facts.body: Manovo-Gounda St Floris combines broad savannahs with northern floodplains. That contrast makes room for very different wildlife communities, from land mammals to waterbirds.

facts.title: Where forest slowly reclaimed savannah
facts.body: Odzala-Kokoua records forest returning to savannah after the ice ages. Forests of different ages meet there, helping explain the park’s exceptional variety of primates and other wildlife.

facts.title: Retreating ice reveals a living experiment
facts.body: In the Jungfrau-Aletsch landscape, retreating glaciers expose fresh ground. Scientists can study the sequence in which plants colonise it, alongside the geological story of the Alps.

facts.title: A river that brings a different habitat
facts.body: The Comoé River allows patches of rainforest to occur much farther north than expected. Its park mixes those forests with savannah vegetation in the same protected landscape.

facts.title: A town built around a staircase
facts.body: Sewell was built so high and steep in the Andes that wheeled vehicles were impractical. Its colourful mining-town buildings grew around a great central staircase instead.

facts.title: A river almost wraps a rainforest
facts.body: The Dja River nearly encircles Cameroon’s Dja Faunal Reserve. This natural boundary surrounds a rainforest refuge with more than a hundred recorded mammal species.

facts.title: A rest stop for millions of birds
facts.body: China’s Yellow Sea and Bohai Gulf wetlands are a bottleneck on a huge migration route. Millions of waterbirds depend on this coastal stopping point between breeding and wintering grounds.

facts.title: A shark gathering far offshore
facts.body: Around remote Malpelo island, observers have recorded groups of more than 200 hammerhead sharks and over 1,000 silky sharks. This little Colombian island sits about 506 km from the coast.

facts.title: A rainforest far out in the Pacific
facts.body: Cocos Island lies about 550 km off Costa Rica. UNESCO identifies it as the tropical eastern Pacific’s only island with a tropical rainforest; underwater, it is famous for large ocean-going animals.

facts.title: Plants that learned to live with toxic rock
facts.body: Some rocks in Alejandro de Humboldt National Park are chemically hostile to plants. Adaptation to those conditions helped produce a remarkable variety of species found nowhere else.

facts.title: An Atlantic town with an early tropical chapter
facts.body: Cidade Velha, formerly Ribeira Grande, is identified by UNESCO as the first European colonial outpost in the tropics. Parts of its early street layout survive on Santiago island.

facts.title: Plain outside, spectacular inside
facts.body: The rural exteriors of some Troodos churches look modest. Inside, elaborate Byzantine and later murals cover the walls—a striking contrast preserved across ten listed monuments.

facts.title: A landscape designed like a garden
facts.body: The Lednice-Valtice estate covers about 200 square kilometres. Its rulers reshaped whole stretches of countryside, combining castles and Baroque buildings with English-inspired romantic landscaping.

facts.title: Ice Age people made music too
facts.body: Caves in Germany’s Swabian Jura have yielded musical instruments as well as carved animals and jewellery. The finds date back roughly 33,000–43,000 years.

facts.title: A landscape of natural chimneys
facts.body: Around Lake Abbe, mineral deposits have built tall chimney-like rock formations. The hot-spring landscape looks industrial, but its towers are geological creations.

facts.title: A prehistoric aquarium in the cliffs
facts.body: The cliffs of western Limfjord preserve exceptionally detailed fossil fish, along with turtles, birds and insects. These remains reveal how life responded to a major warming episode in the early Eocene.

facts.title: A lake that boils
facts.body: Dominica’s Morne Trois Pitons National Park contains a boiling lake, hot springs and dozens of steam vents. Its tropical forest grows across a remarkably active volcanic landscape.

facts.title: A city used as a planning template
facts.body: Santo Domingo’s colonial grid became a model for later towns across the Americas. UNESCO also records the city’s early cathedral, hospital, customs house and university as regional firsts.

facts.title: The Sahara has a picture archive
facts.body: Tassili n’Ajjer holds more than 15,000 prehistoric drawings and engravings. They record changing animals, people and climate in a landscape that looks very different today.

facts.title: Three currents, one evolutionary laboratory
facts.body: Three ocean currents meet around the Galápagos. Combined with volcanic activity and isolation, that setting helped produce the unusual wildlife that influenced Darwin after his 1835 visit.

facts.title: A medieval trading city still readable today
facts.body: Tallinn’s old town grew rich through the Hanseatic trading network. Its surviving merchants’ houses and public buildings let you trace that commercial world through the streets.

facts.title: Whales with legs—in the desert
facts.body: Egypt’s Whale Valley preserves fossils of early whales during their transition from land to sea. Some show the stage when these animals were losing their hind limbs.

facts.title: Modernist architecture high in Africa
facts.body: Asmara sits more than 2,000 metres above sea level and preserves an extensive early-modernist cityscape. Cinemas, hotels and religious buildings reflect a major 1930s building programme under Italian colonial rule.

facts.title: Spain’s highest peak is off Africa
facts.body: Teide stands on Tenerife in the Canary Islands. The volcanic structure rises roughly 7,500 metres from the ocean floor, much farther than the summit’s height above sea level suggests.

facts.title: A goat with a very small world
facts.body: The Walia ibex is found only in Ethiopia’s Simien Mountains. The same landscape has cliffs dropping around 1,500 metres and wildlife adapted to its dramatic high-altitude terrain.

facts.title: An industrial time capsule
facts.body: Verla preserves a rural paper-and-board mill settlement of a kind once widespread across northern Europe and North America. Only a handful of comparable settlements survived so completely.

facts.title: Fiji’s first colonial capital was not Suva
facts.body: It was Levuka, a port town along the beach on Ovalau. Its layout grew around existing indigenous villages, whose residents continued to outnumber European settlers.

facts.title: A city built on artificial islets
facts.body: Nan Madol is spread across more than 100 constructed islets off Pohnpei. Walls of basalt and coral boulders supported palaces, temples and homes built between roughly 1200 and 1500.

facts.title: France has a penguin chapter
facts.body: Remote French islands in the southern Indian Ocean support enormous colonies of king penguins. French geography reaches far beyond Europe into sub-Antarctic seas.

facts.title: Waterfalls with their own miniature worlds
facts.body: Ivindo National Park’s rivers and waterfalls shelter highly localised aquatic plants. UNESCO notes that parts remain little studied and some fish species have yet to be formally described.

facts.title: A penguin with a knighthood
facts.body: Edinburgh Zoo is home to a king penguin called Major General Sir Nils Olav. The zoo identifies him as the world’s only knighted penguin—an unusually distinguished resident of a penguin enclosure.

facts.title: An art gallery you snorkel through
facts.body: Grenada’s Molinere Beauséjour marine area contains an underwater sculpture gallery. The works draw on local culture, moving the idea of a museum visit beneath the sea.

facts.title: A monastery that was also an academy
facts.body: Founded in 1106, Gelati was a major centre of science and education in medieval Georgia. Its academy made the monastery a place for scholarship as well as worship.

facts.title: An Atlantic archive built in stone
facts.body: Ghana’s coastal forts and trading posts were built across more than 300 years, from 1482 to 1786. Their remains mark successive phases of Atlantic trade and European expansion.

facts.title: A small island with a long historical reach
facts.body: Kunta Kinteh Island sits in the River Gambia. Its remains record successive chapters of African–European contact, including the slave trade and its abolition.

facts.title: Tool-using chimpanzees and unusual toads
facts.body: Mount Nimba shelters chimpanzees that use stones as tools and a toad that gives birth to live young. Its mountain habitats rise above the surrounding savannah.

facts.title: Spanish in Central Africa
facts.body: Spanish is one of Equatorial Guinea’s official languages, alongside French and Portuguese. That linguistic combination reflects a very different colonial history from many of its neighbours.

facts.title: The gods had a real mountain address
facts.body: Mount Olympus is a real Greek mountain landscape, not merely a mythical place. Ancient writers made it the home of the Olympian gods, while its steep terrain shelters varied habitats.

facts.title: A crossroads between civilizations
facts.body: Tak’alik Ab’aj records about 1,700 years of history spanning the transition from Olmec to early Maya culture. Trade carried ideas through the site as well as goods.

facts.title: An island stopover for a huge bird migration
facts.body: The Bijagós protected landscape supports over 870,000 migratory shorebirds. It is also part of the only active deltaic archipelago on Africa’s Atlantic coast.

facts.title: A waterfall with a 226-metre plunge
facts.body: Kaieteur Falls drops about 226 metres in Guyana’s rainforest. It is an immense single plunge rather than a long staircase of smaller cascades.

facts.title: Mountains that run down to the Caribbean
facts.body: The Río Plátano reserve links mountainous rainforest to the Caribbean shore. Its landscape is also a long-standing home for indigenous communities, rather than an uninhabited wilderness.

facts.title: A cathedral with 71 faces
facts.body: The Cathedral of St James in Šibenik has a frieze of 71 sculpted faces of women, men and children. Its builders also constructed the cathedral entirely from stone.

facts.title: A fortress built after a revolution
facts.body: Haiti’s Citadel and Sans Souci belong to the years after independence. UNESCO recognises these monuments as symbols of the freedom won by formerly enslaved people.

facts.title: A school inside a thousand-year-old community
facts.body: Benedictine monks settled at Pannonhalma in 996 and established Hungary’s first school. The abbey’s long educational tradition continues alongside its monastic life.

facts.title: From tropical sea to snowy mountains
facts.body: Lorentz National Park spans environments from marine waters and wetlands to high mountain terrain shaped by glaciers. It is a startling reminder that Indonesia has an alpine world as well as tropical islands.

facts.title: Stone-age art on a monumental scale
facts.body: The Boyne Valley’s Newgrange, Knowth and Dowth form an exceptional concentration of prehistoric stone art. These monuments served social and ceremonial roles as well as burial functions.

facts.title: Half a million years in four caves
facts.body: The Mount Carmel caves preserve evidence spanning at least 500,000 years of human evolution. Finds include both Neanderthals and early modern humans within the same broad prehistoric cultural tradition.

facts.title: Bridges made from living roots
facts.body: In Meghalaya, communities guide and weave the living roots of rubber fig trees across streams. Over time, the roots form usable bridges—a piece of infrastructure that is still alive.

facts.title: A wetland world in an arid country
facts.body: Southern Iraq’s Ahwar is a vast inland delta of marshes in a very hot, dry region. Nearby are the remains of Ur, Uruk and Eridu, cities of ancient Mesopotamia.

facts.title: A thousand-year-old brick skyscraper
facts.body: Gonbad-e Qābus is a 53-metre tomb tower built in 1006. Its tapering cylinder and conical roof demonstrate sophisticated geometry using ordinary unglazed fired bricks.

facts.title: An island with a birth date
facts.body: Surtsey emerged from volcanic eruptions between 1963 and 1967. Protected from ordinary human disturbance, it lets scientists watch plants and animals colonise brand-new land.

facts.title: A volcano with a very long written record
facts.body: Mount Etna’s activity has been documented for at least 2,700 years. Its much longer geological record reaches back roughly half a million years.

facts.title: Mountains that became a refuge
facts.body: Jamaica’s Blue and John Crow Mountains sheltered Taino people and later Maroon communities escaping slavery. Trails, settlements and forest knowledge helped communities resist colonial control.

facts.title: Monks who lived on towers
facts.body: At Um er-Rasas, two surviving towers are associated with stylites: ascetic monks who isolated themselves on top of columns or towers. The site also contains elaborate mosaic floors.

facts.title: Wooden buildings from the seventh century
facts.body: Some Buddhist buildings at Horyu-ji date to the late 600s or early 700s. They are among the world’s oldest surviving wooden structures—not stone ruins, but timber architecture.

facts.title: A flamingo feeding destination
facts.body: Kenya’s Rift Valley lakes are crucial feeding grounds for lesser flamingos. Bogoria, Nakuru and Elementaita form a linked lake system supporting extraordinary bird diversity.

facts.title: A mountain home for fruit ancestors
facts.body: The Western Tien-Shan is an important centre of origin for cultivated fruit crops. These mountain forests are part of the deeper story behind familiar fruit on a dinner table.

facts.title: Cambodian temples before Angkor
facts.body: Sambor Prei Kuk has more than 100 temples, including ten unusual octagonal ones. The site belonged to an earlier Khmer capital that flourished before the famous Angkor period.

facts.title: Mountains hidden under the Pacific
facts.body: Kiribati’s Phoenix Islands protected area includes 14 known underwater seamounts, thought to be extinct volcanoes. Its ocean habitats cover over 400,000 square kilometres.

facts.title: Island cities shaped by both family lines
facts.body: The historic Comorian sultanate towns developed with matrilineal and matrilocal customs alongside patrilineal Islamic traditions. Their streets and buildings reflect centuries of Indian Ocean cultural exchange.

facts.title: A Caribbean fortress with a human story
facts.body: Brimstone Hill’s imposing defences were designed by the British and built through the labour of enslaved Africans. The surviving fortress records both military engineering and the people forced to construct it.

facts.title: Ancient daily life painted on tomb walls
facts.body: Some Koguryo tombs preserve murals showing a world that left few other remains. Painted tombs are rare among the thousands discovered across Korea and China.

facts.title: Volcanoes made an underground tunnel network
facts.body: Jeju’s lava tubes preserve passages once occupied by flowing lava. The island also has a volcanic crater lake on Mount Halla and a dramatic tuff cone rising beside the sea.

facts.title: An oil economy that started saving early
facts.body: Kuwait is home to the oldest sovereign wealth fund. Its overseas investment tradition shows how an oil-producing country can turn resource revenue into assets beyond its own borders.

facts.title: A grand building left unfinished
facts.body: The Yasawi mausoleum was begun under Timur in 1389 and remained partly unfinished. Its builders tested architectural ideas later used in the empire’s great capital, Samarkand.

facts.title: Two architectural worlds in one town
facts.body: Luang Prabang blends traditional Lao buildings and urban patterns with French colonial architecture. The combination is preserved across a whole townscape, not just a single landmark.

facts.title: Trees once prized for great buildings
facts.body: Lebanon’s surviving cedar forests connect to an ancient building material traded and valued across the region. Nearby Qadisha’s monasteries cling to a dramatic mountain valley.

facts.title: Twin peaks above a hidden reef world
facts.body: Saint Lucia’s Pitons rise dramatically above the sea, but the protected area continues underwater. Coral reefs occupy almost 60% of its marine portion.

facts.title: A familiar tune with different words
facts.body: Liechtenstein’s national anthem uses the same melody as “God Save the King.” At an international sporting event, the tune can sound British even when the team is not.

facts.title: Paintings across a cave monastery
facts.body: Dambulla’s five cave sanctuaries contain 157 statues and roughly 2,100 square metres of Buddhist murals. The site has been a place of pilgrimage for more than two millennia.

facts.title: An anthem writer who became president
facts.body: Daniel Bashiel Warner wrote the words of Liberia’s national anthem. He later became the country’s third president—a rather unusual career change for a lyricist.

facts.title: A mountain kingdom with rock-art galleries
facts.body: Lesotho shares the Maloti-Drakensberg landscape with South Africa. Its cliffs, caves and rock shelters preserve a remarkable concentration of paintings as well as highland wildlife.

facts.title: A capital that transformed a provincial town
facts.body: Kaunas served as Lithuania’s provisional capital between the world wars. That role triggered a wave of modernist public buildings, homes and urban planning in just two decades.

facts.title: A fortress repeatedly upgraded by its owners
facts.body: Luxembourg’s strategic position made successive European powers reinforce its defences. Centuries of fortification ended with the dismantling of its walls beginning in 1867.

facts.title: Survey markers that helped measure Earth
facts.body: Latvia is on the Struve Geodetic Arc, a 2,820-km chain of survey points across ten countries. Nineteenth-century measurements along it helped establish Earth’s size and shape.

facts.title: A desert city with streets under the houses
facts.body: In Ghadamès, homes overhang covered alleys, creating sheltered passageways. Traditionally, supplies were kept below, families lived above, and women used the open rooftop terraces.

facts.title: Two very different city plans side by side
facts.body: Rabat combines medieval walls and monuments with a large planned city built under the French protectorate. Its urban landscape lets you read two very different eras together.

facts.title: A tiny country with its own anthem language
facts.body: Monaco’s official anthem lyrics are in Monegasque, not French. Its music was adopted in 1867, while the official words followed in 1931.

facts.title: A national anthem edited from a poem
facts.body: Moldova’s anthem began as a twelve-verse poem about language. The official song selects verses 1, 2, 5, 9 and 12 rather than simply using the opening verses.

facts.title: Glaciers above, rivers below
facts.body: Durmitor’s dramatic landscape was carved by glaciers, then cut by rivers and underground streams. The Tara canyon is among Europe’s deepest gorges.

facts.title: An evolutionary experiment lasting millions of years
facts.body: Madagascar’s long isolation helped its plants and animals evolve independently. Its eastern rainforests preserve part of that distinctive world, including rare lemurs.

facts.title: History beneath a lagoon
facts.body: Bikini Atoll’s lagoon contains ships sunk during the 1946 nuclear tests. These underwater remains are part of a difficult history that also includes the displacement of the islanders.

facts.title: A lake with ancient survivors
facts.body: Lake Ohrid shelters freshwater species with very old evolutionary lineages. Around its shores, archaeological evidence also records prehistoric settlements built on piles over the water.

facts.title: A pyramid built from mud
facts.body: The Tomb of Askia in Gao has a striking 17-metre pyramidal form. Built in 1495, it reflects the wealth of the Songhai Empire and the Sahel’s monumental earthen-building tradition.

facts.title: A whole landscape of sacred architecture
facts.body: Bagan was a major imperial capital between the eleventh and thirteenth centuries. Its temples, stupas, monasteries and wall paintings preserve the scale of that Buddhist civilisation.

facts.title: A landscape that changes with climate cycles
facts.body: Dauria’s alternating wet and dry periods create shifting habitats of grassland, forest, lakes and wetlands. These support migratory birds and the cross-border movements of Mongolian gazelles.

facts.title: Desert dunes meet a bird-filled sea
facts.body: At Banc d’Arguin, Sahara dunes sit beside shallow Atlantic waters, islands and coastal swamps. That abrupt meeting of desert and ocean creates a major wintering ground for migratory birds.

facts.title: Hundreds of monuments in a tiny capital
facts.body: UNESCO counts 320 monuments within Valletta’s 55 hectares. Malta’s capital packs an extraordinary amount of architectural history into a very small footprint.

facts.title: A mountain that became a symbol of freedom
facts.body: Escaped enslaved people sheltered on Le Morne’s wooded cliffs and in its caves. Their history gave this Mauritian mountain a meaning far beyond its dramatic outline.

facts.title: A cabinet meeting in scuba gear
facts.body: In October 2009, Maldivian ministers held a cabinet meeting four metres underwater. The event was designed to draw attention to climate change before the Copenhagen summit.

facts.title: A mountain rising like an island
facts.body: Mount Mulanje is an enormous inselberg—a mountain mass rising above the surrounding landscape. For local communities, its water, rocks and forests also belong to a sacred landscape.

facts.title: A forest made of cacti
facts.body: The Tehuacán-Cuicatlán Valley has exceptionally dense forests of tall columnar cacti. It also preserves ancient canals, wells and dams that supported early agricultural settlements.

facts.title: A room hundreds of metres wide—underground
facts.body: Sarawak Chamber in Gunung Mulu is about 600 metres long, 415 metres wide and 80 metres high. The surrounding cave network is home to millions of bats and swiftlets.

facts.title: Coral reefs and savannah in one protected landscape
facts.body: The Maputo–iSimangaliso coastal region crosses Mozambique and South Africa. Its habitats range from reefs and seagrass to freshwater lakes, mangroves and savannah.

facts.title: A desert that drinks fog
facts.body: In the Namib Sand Sea, fog is the principal source of water. Animals adapted to it live among dunes made from material transported by rivers, ocean currents and wind.

facts.title: A mountain refuge surrounded by the Sahara
facts.body: The volcanic Aïr massif forms a pocket of different climate, plants and animals within the Ténéré desert. The reserve protects that contrast between mountain refuge and vast desert.

facts.title: A forest that is also an art landscape
facts.body: The Osun-Osogbo Sacred Grove contains shrines, sculptures and sanctuaries among its trees and river bends. It preserves a Yoruba tradition of sacred forests once widespread around settlements.

facts.title: A colonial town whose growth stopped
facts.body: León Viejo never developed into a modern city on the same site. That makes its ruins an unusually clear record of an early Spanish settlement’s layout and society.

facts.title: Amsterdam’s canals were a city-building system
facts.body: The canal ring was a planned expansion onto drained marshland. Concentric waterways and the spaces between them created new neighbourhoods and became an influential model of urban planning.

facts.title: A cliff that continues under the sea
facts.body: The walls of Geirangerfjord and Nærøyfjord rise as much as 1,400 metres above the water and extend around 500 metres below sea level. The visible cliff is only part of the landscape.

facts.title: Everest shares a home with red pandas
facts.body: Sagarmatha National Park is famous for Everest, but it also protects rare wildlife such as red pandas and snow leopards. Its habitats extend through valleys, forests and high mountain terrain.

facts.title: An island with a distinctive language
facts.body: Nauru developed in considerable isolation because currents made landing difficult. Its language does not closely resemble those of neighbouring Pacific societies, according to the Factbook’s historical account.

facts.title: A parrot that lives in the mountains
facts.body: New Zealand’s kea is the world’s only alpine parrot. It lives in a landscape that also contains forests with trees more than 800 years old.

facts.title: A tree resin that powered trade routes
facts.body: Frankincense helped connect Oman’s trees, desert caravan stops and ports to the wider ancient world. The Land of Frankincense sites preserve several parts of that trading system.

facts.title: A natural bridge between continents
facts.body: Darién links the ecosystems of North and South America. Within one national park are beaches, mangroves, swamps and both lowland and upland tropical forests.

facts.title: Tropical mountains with glaciers
facts.body: Peru’s Cordillera Blanca is the world’s highest tropical mountain range. Huascarán National Park combines glaciers and glacial lakes with wildlife such as spectacled bears and Andean condors.

facts.title: Agriculture developed here independently
facts.body: At Kuk, people transformed highland wetlands into farmland over thousands of years. Archaeology points to an independent origin of agriculture, including early drainage ditches dug with wooden tools.

facts.title: A mountain with species of its own
facts.body: Mount Hamiguitan shelters plants and animals found nowhere else. Its elevation changes create different habitats within one mountain ridge, including homes for the Philippine eagle and cockatoo.

facts.title: A city remembered through its tombs
facts.body: Thatta was the capital of three successive dynasties before Mughal rule. Its elaborate Makli necropolis preserves the artistic traditions of centuries of Sindh’s history.

facts.title: European bison have a forest stronghold
facts.body: Białowieża Forest, shared with Belarus, protects the largest population of European bison. Its old forest includes both broadleaf trees and conifers.

facts.title: Sharing spring water by tradition
facts.body: Battir’s terraced gardens are fed by channels carrying water from underground sources. A traditional allocation system shares the collected water among village families.

facts.title: An aqueduct built to outlast a siege
facts.body: Elvas’s defences include the Amoreira aqueduct, which helped supply the fortified town during long sieges. Its elaborate dry-ditch fortifications form an enormous interconnected defensive system.

facts.title: Seawater lakes cut off from the sea
facts.body: Palau’s Rock Islands have an exceptional concentration of marine lakes: seawater enclosed by land. Their isolation has supported distinctive populations and continuing species discoveries.

facts.title: Ruins of a different kind of planned community
facts.body: The Jesuit missions at Trinidad and Jesús preserve more than churches. They are remains of settlements built around religious, social and economic projects in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries.

facts.title: Before gas, there were pearls
facts.body: Al Zubarah prospered through pearl diving and trade in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. Windblown desert sand later protected the abandoned town’s streets, homes and harbour remains.

facts.title: Rome’s province beyond the Danube
facts.body: Dacia was the Roman Empire’s only province entirely north of the Danube. Its frontier in today’s Romania operated from 106 to 271 CE and left forts, watchtowers and ramparts.

facts.title: Serbia’s capital before Belgrade
facts.body: Stari Ras was an early Serbian capital. Its surrounding churches, monasteries and fortifications preserve connections between the medieval Byzantine and western European worlds.

facts.title: An Arctic island the ice sheets missed
facts.body: Wrangel Island was not covered by glaciers during the Quaternary Ice Age. That history helped it retain unusually rich Arctic biodiversity, including hundreds of plant species.

facts.title: A rainforest with peat bogs and moors
facts.body: Nyungwe is more than a forest of tall trees: it also includes peat bogs, grasslands and moorland. This mix helps support hundreds of bird species and rare mammals.

facts.title: An oasis with millions of palms
facts.body: Al-Ahsa contains about 2.5 million date palms. Its canals, springs, wells and gardens show how generations built a settled landscape in an arid region.

facts.title: A coral lagoon that became a lake
facts.body: Lake Tegano on Rennell Island was once an atoll lagoon. The island’s uplift left a large brackish lake surrounded by limestone and forest.

facts.title: A giant-tortoise stronghold
facts.body: Remote Aldabra supports an extraordinary population of giant tortoises. Its four main coral islands surround a lagoon, and difficult access has helped limit human disturbance.

facts.title: Dugongs off the desert coast
facts.body: Sudan’s Dungonab Bay supports a significant dugong population. Along this Red Sea coast, mangroves, seagrass beds and coral reefs create a very different world from the desert inland.

facts.title: A coastline still rising out of the sea
facts.body: Sweden’s High Coast is rebounding after the weight of ice-age glaciers was removed. Along the shared High Coast–Kvarken landscape, land rises, islands join and bays can become lakes.

facts.title: A garden that helped change an industry
facts.body: Singapore Botanic Gardens became a major centre for rubber cultivation research. A garden in the city helped shape plantation agriculture across Southeast Asia.

facts.title: Waterfalls inside the Earth
facts.body: Škocjan’s limestone cave system contains underground waterfalls and around six kilometres of passages. The surrounding Kras region helped give the term “karst” to this type of landscape.

facts.title: Different traditions, one building material
facts.body: Eight listed Carpathian churches show how Catholic, Protestant and eastern Christian communities expressed their architecture in wood. Their designs adapted to local conditions and different worship practices.

facts.title: A rainforest home for small hippos
facts.body: The Gola-Tiwai landscape shelters pygmy hippopotamuses as well as forest elephants. It also supports more than a thousand plant species and hundreds of bird species.

facts.title: A medieval republic that kept going
facts.body: San Marino’s historic centre preserves the institutions of a free republic dating from the Middle Ages. Its government still operates within a cityscape shaped by Mount Titano.

facts.title: An antelope on a giant scale
facts.body: Niokolo-Koba shelters the giant eland, among the largest antelopes. Its river-fed forests and savannahs also create habitats for chimpanzees and many other animals.

facts.title: A painted cattle gallery in the rocks
facts.body: The Laas Geel rock shelters near Hargeisa, in Somaliland, preserve vivid prehistoric cattle paintings. The artwork records a pastoral world thousands of years before modern borders.

facts.title: Dutch-speaking South America
facts.body: Dutch is Suriname’s official language, while Sranan Tongo is widely used as a common language. The country’s linguistic mix connects South America with the Netherlands, Africa and Asia.

facts.title: Millions of animals on the move
facts.body: South Sudan’s Boma–Badingilo landscape supports a vast migration of antelopes. Seasonal rainfall and flooding drive animals between connected grasslands, wetlands and savannahs.

facts.title: Plantations organised like miniature towns
facts.body: The roças combined fields, processing machinery, housing and social facilities in planned complexes. They reveal how coffee and cocoa production shaped island life, including the coercion of colonial labour.

facts.title: A farming village frozen by a volcano
facts.body: Joya de Cerén was buried by an eruption around 600 CE. Like Pompeii, its exceptional preservation offers a close look at ordinary lives—in this case a Central American farming community.

facts.title: Whole villages from late antiquity
facts.body: Northern Syria’s listed ancient villages preserve homes, baths, cisterns and religious buildings. Their layouts reveal rural life and agricultural engineering many centuries before modern towns.

facts.title: A national anthem with two musical influences
facts.body: Eswatini’s anthem combines Swazi and western musical elements. Adopted at independence in 1968, it is a small musical record of traditions meeting.

facts.title: Fresh water in the Sahara
facts.body: Chad’s Ounianga site has 18 lakes fed by groundwater in an extremely dry desert. Some are salty, while others support freshwater fish; floating reeds help limit evaporation.

facts.title: Homes shaped like small towers
facts.body: The Batammariba of Koutammakou build remarkable earthen tower-houses. The architecture is tied to social life and a landscape of farmland, sacred rocks, springs and ceremonial places.

facts.title: Stones that mark sacred space
facts.body: At Phu Phrabat, stone boundary markers and modified rock shelters turned a natural landscape into a Buddhist religious centre. Rock paintings also record occupation stretching back more than two millennia.

facts.title: A forest fed by rivers in dry country
facts.body: Tigrovaya Balka protects rare tugay floodplain forests. Asiatic poplars survive here in a river-fed ecosystem surrounded by desert and mountain landscapes.

facts.title: An island explained by a crocodile
facts.body: In a Timorese creation legend, a crocodile repays a boy’s kindness and ultimately becomes the island of Timor. Crocodiles are consequently addressed as “Grandfather” in this tradition.

facts.title: Four thousand years in an oasis
facts.body: Ancient Merv is a succession of cities within one Silk Road oasis. Its extensive remains record about 4,000 years of human history.

facts.title: A Punic city without a Roman rebuild
facts.body: Kerkuane was abandoned around the time of the First Punic War. Because the Romans did not rebuild it, the surviving plan offers a rare view of a Phoenician-Punic town.

facts.title: A small island kingdom with a far-reaching past
facts.body: By around 1200, Tonga’s rulers had extended influence far across Polynesia and into parts of Melanesia and Micronesia. The modern kingdom is much smaller than that old network of influence.

facts.title: A city linked to the beginnings of coinage
facts.body: Sardis was the capital of wealthy Lydia, known for early coin production. Nearby Bin Tepe contains some of the world’s largest ancient burial mounds.

facts.title: Music made from oil drums
facts.body: Trinidad and Tobago’s steelpan grew out of experiments with metal containers and discarded oil drums. Careful shaping and tuning turned an industrial object into a melodic instrument.

facts.title: An internet address that earns money
facts.body: The “.tv” internet domain belongs to Tuvalu. Licensing the domain provides income for a tiny Pacific country whose online address is recognised far beyond its islands.

facts.title: Footprints older than our species
facts.body: The Ngorongoro area preserves evidence of early human relatives, including footprints about 3.6 million years old. Its story reaches far beyond the wildlife visible there today.

facts.title: A cathedral imagined as a new Constantinople
facts.body: Kyiv’s Saint-Sophia Cathedral was designed to rival Hagia Sophia. It expressed the ambitions of an eleventh-century capital through architecture and religious art.

facts.title: An alpine world near the equator
facts.body: The Rwenzori Mountains have high-altitude landscapes with lakes, waterfalls and giant heather. Mount Margherita rises above 5,000 metres, creating a very different Uganda from the lowlands.

facts.title: Hundreds of miles beneath Kentucky
facts.body: Kentucky’s Mammoth Cave is the world’s longest known cave system, with hundreds of miles of mapped passages. Explorers have repeatedly connected neighbouring systems, revealing an even larger underground network.

facts.title: A town that helped feed distant continents
facts.body: Fray Bentos processed cattle from nearby grasslands into meat extract and corned beef for export to Europe. The surviving industrial landscape shows the whole chain from processing to shipment.

facts.title: A Silk Road city with an observatory
facts.body: Samarkand’s famous monuments include Ulugh Beg’s observatory as well as mosques and madrasas. Scholarship and astronomy were part of the city’s cultural world, alongside trade.

facts.title: A whole country on the heritage list
facts.body: Vatican City itself is a UNESCO World Heritage property. Within this tiny state are palaces, gardens, St Peter’s Basilica and works associated with artists including Michelangelo and Bernini.

facts.title: A garden older than many modern countries
facts.body: Saint Vincent’s Botanic Gardens was founded in 1765. It began as a centre for studying and exchanging medicinal plants and became an important conservation and research site.

facts.title: Mountains shaped like giant tables
facts.body: Canaima’s tepuis are steep-sided, flat-topped mountains. Their cliffs and waterfalls, including Angel Falls, create a landscape very different from the pointed peaks people usually imagine.

facts.title: Rivers that disappear underground
facts.body: The Phong Nha-Ke Bang–Hin Nam No karst landscape spans Vietnam and Laos. Hundreds of kilometres of caves and underground waterways have been documented in this ancient limestone terrain.

facts.title: Oral history meets archaeology
facts.body: Sites associated with Chief Roi Mata preserve places linked to his life, death and burial. Archaeological evidence and living oral traditions tell connected versions of this Vanuatu history.

facts.title: The country that skipped a Friday
facts.body: Samoa went straight from 29 to 31 December in 2011 when it changed sides of the International Date Line. Friday, 30 December never occurred there that year.

facts.title: An island group full of local originals
facts.body: A large share of Socotra’s plants and reptiles occur nowhere else. UNESCO records endemism in about 37% of its plant species and 90% of its reptile species.

facts.title: A scar from two billion years ago
facts.body: Vredefort preserves part of a vast meteorite impact structure formed about 2.02 billion years ago. Erosion has exposed a deep cross-section of that ancient collision.

facts.title: A waterfall you can see before you see it
facts.body: The spray from Victoria Falls can be visible more than 20 kilometres away. The Zambezi plunges through basalt gorges, producing the mist behind its name Mosi-oa-Tunya.

facts.title: A medieval city in southern Africa
facts.body: Great Zimbabwe was a major Shona trading centre between the eleventh and fifteenth centuries. Its extensive stone ruins challenge the idea that medieval urban history belongs only to Europe and Asia.

facts.title: The shape of United Arab Emirates
facts.body: Flat, barren coastal plain merging into rolling sand dunes of vast desert; mountains in east

facts.title: The shape of Antigua and Barbuda
facts.body: Mostly low-lying limestone and coral islands, with some higher volcanic areas

facts.title: The shape of Armenia
facts.body: Armenian Highland with mountains; little forest land; fast flowing rivers; good soil in Aras River valley

facts.title: The shape of Argentina
facts.body: Rich plains of the Pampas in northern half, flat to rolling plateau of Patagonia in south, rugged Andes along western border

facts.title: The shape of Austria
facts.body: Mostly mountains (Alps) in the west and south; mostly flat or gently sloping along the eastern and northern margins

facts.title: The shape of Azerbaijan
facts.body: Large, flat Kur-Araz Ovaligi (Kura-Araks Lowland, much of it below sea level) with Great Caucasus Mountains to the north, Qarabag Yaylasi (Karabakh Upland) to the west; Baku lies on Abseron Yasaqligi (Apsheron Peninsula) that juts into Caspian Sea

facts.title: The shape of Belgium
facts.body: Flat coastal plains in northwest, central rolling hills, rugged mountains of Ardennes Forest in southeast

facts.title: The shape of Burkina Faso
facts.body: Mostly flat to dissected, undulating plains; hills in the west and southeast; occupies an extensive plateau with savanna that is grassy in the north and gradually gives way to sparse forests in the south

facts.title: The shape of Burundi
facts.body: Hilly and mountainous, dropping to a plateau in east, some plains

facts.title: The shape of Brunei
facts.body: Flat coastal plain rises to mountains in east; hilly lowland in west

facts.title: The shape of Bolivia
facts.body: Rugged Andes Mountains with a highland plateau (Altiplano), hills, lowland plains of the Amazon Basin

facts.title: The shape of Brazil
facts.body: Mostly flat to rolling lowlands in north; some plains, hills, mountains, and narrow coastal belt

facts.title: The shape of Botswana
facts.body: Predominantly flat to gently rolling tableland; Kalahari Desert in southwest

facts.title: The shape of Central African Republic
facts.body: Vast, flat to rolling plateau; scattered hills in northeast and southwest

facts.title: The shape of Switzerland
facts.body: Mostly mountains (Alps in south, Jura in northwest) with a central plateau of rolling hills, plains, and large lakes

facts.title: The shape of Chile
facts.body: Low coastal mountains, fertile central valley, rugged Andes in east

facts.title: The shape of Cameroon
facts.body: Diverse, with coastal plain in southwest, dissected plateau in center, mountains in west, plains in north

facts.title: The shape of China
facts.body: Mostly mountains, high plateaus, deserts in west; plains, deltas, and hills in east

facts.title: The shape of Colombia
facts.body: Flat coastal lowlands, central highlands, high Andes Mountains, eastern lowland plains (Llanos)

facts.title: The shape of Costa Rica
facts.body: Coastal plains separated by rugged mountains including over 100 volcanic cones, of which several are major active volcanoes

facts.title: The shape of Cuba
facts.body: Mostly flat to rolling plains, with rugged hills and mountains in the southeast

facts.title: The shape of Cyprus
facts.body: Central plain with mountains to north and south; scattered but significant plains along southern coast

facts.title: The shape of Czechia
facts.body: Bohemia in the west consists of rolling plains, hills, and plateaus surrounded by low mountains; Moravia in the east consists of very hilly country

facts.title: The shape of Algeria
facts.body: Mostly high plateau and desert; Atlas Mountains in the far north and Hoggar Mountains in the south; narrow, discontinuous coastal plain

facts.title: The shape of Ecuador
facts.body: Coastal plain (costa), inter-Andean central highlands (sierra), and flat to rolling eastern jungle (oriente)

facts.title: The shape of Eritrea
facts.body: Dominated by extension of Ethiopian north-south trending highlands, descending on the east to a coastal desert plain, on the northwest to hilly terrain and on the southwest to flat-to-rolling plains

facts.title: The shape of Spain
facts.body: Large, flat to dissected plateau surrounded by rugged hills; Pyrenees Mountains in north

facts.title: The shape of Ethiopia
facts.body: High plateau with central mountain range divided by Great Rift Valley

facts.title: The shape of Finland
facts.body: Mostly low, flat to rolling plains interspersed with lakes and low hills

facts.title: The shape of Micronesia
facts.body: Islands vary geologically from high mountainous islands to low, coral atolls; volcanic outcroppings on Pohnpei, Kosrae, and Chuuk

facts.title: The shape of France
facts.body: Metropolitan France: mostly flat plains or gently rolling hills in north and west; remainder is mountainous, especially Pyrenees in south, Alps in east French Guiana: low-lying coastal plains rising to hills and small mountains Guadeloupe: Basse-Terre is volcanic in origin with interior mountains; Grande-Terre is low limestone formation; most of the seven other islands are volcanic in origin Martinique: mountainous with indented coastline; dormant volcano Mayotte: generally undulating, with deep ravines and ancient volcanic peaks Reunion: mostly rugged and mountainous; fertile lowlands along coast

facts.title: The shape of United Kingdom
facts.body: Mostly rugged hills and low mountains; level to rolling plains in east and southeast

facts.title: The shape of Georgia
facts.body: Largely mountainous with Great Caucasus Mountains in the north and Lesser Caucasus Mountains in the south; Kolkhet'is Dablobi (Kolkhida Lowland) opens to the Black Sea in the west; Mtkvari River Basin in the east; fertile soils in river valley flood plains and foothills of Kolkhida Lowland

facts.title: The shape of Greece
facts.body: Mountainous with ranges extending into the sea as peninsulas or chains of islands

facts.title: The shape of Guatemala
facts.body: Two east-west trending mountain chains divide the country into three regions: the mountainous highlands, the Pacific coast south of mountains, and the vast northern Peten lowlands

facts.title: The shape of Guinea-Bissau
facts.body: Mostly low-lying coastal plain with a deeply indented estuarine coastline rising to savanna in east; numerous off-shore islands including the Arquipelago Dos Bijagos consisting of 18 main islands and many small islets

facts.title: The shape of Croatia
facts.body: Geographically diverse; flat plains along Hungarian border, low mountains and highlands near Adriatic coastline and islands

facts.title: The shape of Hungary
facts.body: Mostly flat to rolling plains; hills and low mountains on the Slovakian border

facts.title: The shape of Ireland
facts.body: Mostly flat to rolling interior plain surrounded by rugged hills and low mountains; sea cliffs on west coast

facts.title: The shape of Israel
facts.body: Negev desert in the south; low coastal plain; central mountains; Jordan Rift Valley

facts.title: The shape of India
facts.body: Upland plain (Deccan Plateau) in south, flat to rolling plain along the Ganges, deserts in west, Himalayas in north

facts.title: The shape of Iraq
facts.body: Mostly broad plains; reedy marshes along Iranian border in south with large flooded areas; mountains along borders with Iran and Turkey

facts.title: The shape of Iran
facts.body: Rugged, mountainous rim; high, central basin with deserts, mountains; small, discontinuous plains along both coasts

facts.title: The shape of Iceland
facts.body: Mostly plateau interspersed with mountain peaks, icefields; coast deeply indented by bays and fiords

facts.title: The shape of Jordan
facts.body: Mostly arid desert plateau; a great north-south geological rift along the west of the country is the dominant topographical feature and includes the Jordan River Valley, the Dead Sea, and the Jordanian Highlands

facts.title: The shape of Kenya
facts.body: Low plains rise to central highlands bisected by Great Rift Valley; fertile plateau in west

facts.title: The shape of Kyrgyzstan
facts.body: Peaks of the Tien Shan mountain range and associated valleys and basins encompass the entire country

facts.title: The shape of Comoros
facts.body: Volcanic islands, interiors vary from steep mountains to low hills

facts.title: The shape of North Korea
facts.body: Mostly hills and mountains separated by deep, narrow valleys; wide coastal plains in west, discontinuous in east

facts.title: The shape of South Korea
facts.body: Mostly hills and mountains; wide coastal plains in west and south

facts.title: The shape of Kazakhstan
facts.body: Vast flat steppe extending from the Volga in the west to the Altai Mountains in the east and from the plains of western Siberia in the north to oases and deserts of Central Asia in the south

facts.title: The shape of Lebanon
facts.body: Narrow coastal plain; El Beqaa (Bekaa Valley) separates Lebanon and Anti-Lebanon Mountains

facts.title: The shape of Sri Lanka
facts.body: Mostly low, flat to rolling plain; mountains in south-central interior

facts.title: The shape of Liberia
facts.body: Mostly flat to rolling coastal plains rising to rolling plateau and low mountains in northeast

facts.title: The shape of Luxembourg
facts.body: Mostly gently rolling uplands with broad, shallow valleys; uplands to slightly mountainous in the north; steep slope down to Moselle flood plain in the southeast

facts.title: The shape of Morocco
facts.body: Mountainous northern coast (Rif Mountains) and interior (Atlas Mountains) bordered by large plateaus with intermontane valleys, and fertile coastal plains; the south is mostly low, flat desert with large areas of rocky or sandy surfaces

facts.title: The shape of Montenegro
facts.body: Highly indented coastline with narrow coastal plain backed by rugged high limestone mountains and plateaus

facts.title: The shape of North Macedonia
facts.body: Mountainous with deep basins and valleys; three large lakes, each divided by a frontier line; country bisected by the Vardar River

facts.title: The shape of Mali
facts.body: Mostly flat to rolling northern plains covered by sand; savanna in south, rugged hills in northeast

facts.title: The shape of Mongolia
facts.body: Vast semidesert and desert plains, grassy steppe, mountains in west and southwest; Gobi Desert in south-central

facts.title: The shape of Mauritius
facts.body: Small coastal plain rising to discontinuous mountains encircling central plateau

facts.title: The shape of Maldives
facts.body: Flat coral atolls, with white sandy beaches; sits atop the submarine volcanic Chagos-Laccadive Ridge

facts.title: The shape of Malawi
facts.body: Narrow elongated plateau with rolling plains, rounded hills, some mountains

facts.title: The shape of Mexico
facts.body: High, rugged mountains; low coastal plains; high plateaus; desert

facts.title: The shape of Mozambique
facts.body: Mostly coastal lowlands, uplands in center, high plateaus in northwest, mountains in west

facts.title: The shape of Namibia
facts.body: Mostly high plateau; Namib Desert along coast; Kalahari Desert in east

facts.title: The shape of Niger
facts.body: Predominately desert plains and sand dunes; flat to rolling plains in south; hills in north

facts.title: The shape of Nigeria
facts.body: Southern lowlands merge into central hills and plateaus; mountains in southeast, plains in north

facts.title: The shape of Nicaragua
facts.body: Extensive Atlantic coastal plains rising to central interior mountains; narrow Pacific coastal plain interrupted by volcanoes

facts.title: The shape of Netherlands
facts.body: Mostly coastal lowland and reclaimed land (polders); some hills in southeast

facts.title: The shape of Norway
facts.body: Glaciated; mostly high plateaus and rugged mountains broken by fertile valleys; small, scattered plains; coastline deeply indented by fjords; arctic tundra in north

facts.title: The shape of Nepal
facts.body: Tarai or flat river plain of the Ganges in south; central hill region with rugged Himalayas in north

facts.title: The shape of Nauru
facts.body: Sandy beach rises to fertile ring around raised coral reefs with phosphate plateau in center

facts.title: The shape of Panama
facts.body: Interior mostly steep, rugged mountains with dissected, upland plains; coastal plains with rolling hills

facts.title: The shape of Peru
facts.body: Western coastal plain (costa), high and rugged Andes in center (sierra), eastern lowland jungle of Amazon Basin (selva)

facts.title: The shape of Pakistan
facts.body: Divided into three major geographic areas: the northern highlands, the Indus River plain in the center and east, and the Balochistan Plateau in the south and west

facts.title: The shape of Palestine
facts.body: Mostly rugged, dissected upland in west, flat plains descending to Jordan River Valley to the east

facts.title: The shape of Portugal
facts.body: The west-flowing Tagus River divides the country: the north is mountainous toward the interior, while the south is characterized by rolling plains

facts.title: The shape of Palau
facts.body: Varying topography from the high, mountainous main island of Babelthuap to low, coral islands usually fringed by large barrier reefs

facts.title: The shape of Paraguay
facts.body: Grassy plains and wooded hills east of Rio Paraguay; Gran Chaco region west of Rio Paraguay mostly low, marshy plain near the river, and dry forest and thorny scrub elsewhere

facts.title: The shape of Romania
facts.body: Central Transylvanian Basin is separated from the Moldavian Plateau on the east by the Eastern Carpathian Mountains and separated from the Walachian Plain on the south by the Transylvanian Alps

facts.title: The shape of Serbia
facts.body: Extremely varied; to the north, rich fertile plains; to the east, limestone ranges and basins; to the southeast, ancient mountains and hills

facts.title: The shape of Russia
facts.body: Broad plain with low hills west of Urals; vast coniferous forest and tundra in Siberia; uplands and mountains along southern border regions

facts.title: The shape of Rwanda
facts.body: Mostly grassy uplands and hills; relief is mountainous with altitude declining from west to east

facts.title: The shape of Seychelles
facts.body: Mahe Group is volcanic with a narrow coastal strip and rocky, hilly interior; others are relatively flat coral atolls, or elevated reefs; sits atop the submarine Mascarene Plateau

facts.title: The shape of Slovenia
facts.body: A short southwestern coastal strip of Karst topography on the Adriatic; an alpine mountain region lies adjacent to Italy and Austria in the north; mixed mountains and valleys with numerous rivers to the east

facts.title: The shape of Slovakia
facts.body: Rugged mountains in the central and northern part and lowlands in the south

facts.title: The shape of Sierra Leone
facts.body: Coastal belt of mangrove swamps, wooded hill country, upland plateau, mountains in east

facts.title: The shape of South Sudan
facts.body: Plains in the north and center rise to southern highlands along the border with Uganda and Kenya; the White Nile, flowing north out of the uplands of Central Africa, is the major geographic feature of the country; The Sudd (a name derived from floating vegetation that hinders navigation) is a large swampy area of more than 100,000 sq km fed by the waters of the White Nile that dominates the center of the country

facts.title: The shape of Syria
facts.body: Primarily semiarid and desert plateau; narrow coastal plain; mountains in west

facts.title: The shape of Chad
facts.body: Broad, arid plains in center, desert in north, mountains in northwest, lowlands in south

facts.title: The shape of Togo
facts.body: Gently rolling savanna in north; central hills; southern plateau; low coastal plain with extensive lagoons and marshes

facts.title: The shape of Tajikistan
facts.body: Mountainous region dominated by the Alay Mountains in the north and the Pamirs in the southeast; western Fergana Valley in north, Kofirnihon and Vakhsh Valleys in southwest

facts.title: The shape of Turkmenistan
facts.body: Flat-to-rolling sandy desert with dunes rising to mountains in the south; low mountains along border with Iran; borders Caspian Sea in west

facts.title: The shape of Tunisia
facts.body: Mountains in north; hot, dry central plain; semiarid south merges into the Sahara

facts.title: The shape of Tonga
facts.body: Mostly flat islands with limestone bedrock formed from uplifted coral formation; others have limestone overlying volcanic rock

facts.title: The shape of Türkiye
facts.body: High central plateau (Anatolia); narrow coastal plain; several mountain ranges

facts.title: The shape of Ukraine
facts.body: Mostly fertile plains (steppes) and plateaus, with mountains found only in the west (the Carpathians) or in the extreme south of the Crimean Peninsula

facts.title: The shape of United States
facts.body: Vast central plain, mountains in west, hills and low mountains in east; rugged mountains and broad river valleys in Alaska; rugged, volcanic topography in Hawaii

facts.title: The shape of Uzbekistan
facts.body: Mostly flat-to-rolling sandy desert with dunes; broad, flat intensely irrigated river valleys along course of Amu Darya, Syr Darya (Sirdaryo), and Zaravshan; Fergana Valley in east surrounded by mountainous Tajikistan and Kyrgyzstan; shrinking Aral Sea in west

facts.title: The shape of Venezuela
facts.body: Andes Mountains and Maracaibo Lowlands in northwest; central plains (llanos); Guiana Highlands in southeast

facts.title: The shape of Vietnam
facts.body: Low, flat delta in south and north; central highlands; hilly, mountainous in far north and northwest

facts.title: The shape of Vanuatu
facts.body: Mostly mountainous islands of volcanic origin; narrow coastal plains

facts.title: The shape of Samoa
facts.body: Two main islands (Savaii, Upolu) and several smaller islands and uninhabited islets; narrow coastal plain with volcanic, rugged mountains in interior

facts.title: The shape of Yemen
facts.body: Narrow coastal plain backed by flat-topped hills and rugged mountains; dissected upland desert plains in center slope into the desert interior of the Arabian Peninsula

facts.title: The shape of South Africa
facts.body: Vast interior plateau rimmed by rugged hills and narrow coastal plain

facts.title: The shape of Zimbabwe
facts.body: Mostly high plateau with higher central plateau (high veld); mountains in east

facts.title: The longest mountain range is mostly hidden
facts.body: The mid-ocean ridge stretches about 65,000 km around Earth. Roughly 90% of it is underwater: the world’s longest mountain range is mainly a feature of the seafloor.
